query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled build chamber preheating step during the selective laser melting (SLM) of high-entropy alloys will reduce high thermal gradients, leading to a more homogeneous microstructure, fewer fabrication-induced defects, and improved dimensional precision and mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) produced under standard SLM conditions without preheating, which typically exhibits residual stress-induced distortions and defect zones.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled preheating protocol (e.g., preheating the build chamber or substrate to an optimized intermediate temperature) during SLM processing.
generation.conditions: The intervention should be applied under typical SLM processing parameters for high-entropy alloys at ambient atmospheric conditions, with preheating temperatures calibrated to moderate values (e.g., around 200–300°C) that do not induce oxidation but are high enough to reduce thermal gradients.
generation.structural_mediator: The preheating lowers the thermal gradient during the laser melting and solidification stages, reducing residual stresses and promoting a uniform microstructure with fewer defects such as porosity and micro-cracks.
generation.mechanism: By reducing the temperature differential between the melt pool and the surrounding material, the cooling rate is moderated, thus minimizing thermal shock and residual stresses. This promotes dimensional accuracy by decreasing part warping and improves mechanical integrity by reducing defect-related weaknesses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components fabricated with preheating will exhibit significantly improved dimensional precision (closer adherence to CAD specifications) and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., higher strength and ductility, fewer microstructural defects) relative to those fabricated under standard, room-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: SLM fabrication of the high-entropy alloy without preheating, which is known to produce parts with residual stress issues and higher densities of fabrication-induced defects as observed in prior studies.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis holds under conditions where the preheating temperature is carefully controlled to avoid adverse effects such as oxidation or unwanted phase transformations. It is most applicable to alloy systems processed by SLM that have moderate thermal sensitivities and are not prone to high-temperature degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal preheating temperature range and the precise magnitude of improvements in dimensional precision and mechanical integrity remain uncertain until validated by controlled experiments; additionally, effects may vary with alloy composition and specific SLM parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples using SLM: one set under standard room-temperature conditions and the other under controlled preheating conditions (e.g., build chamber preheated to ~250°C). Ensure all other processing parameters are held constant. Post-fabrication, evaluate the parts for dimensional accuracy, microstructural uniformity, defect density (via microscopy), and mechanical properties (via tensile or compression tests).
measurements: Dimensional deviation from CAD geometry (using high-precision metrology tools)
Residual stress analysis (e.g., X-ray diffraction residual stress mapping)
Microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM to quantify porosity, microcracks, and grain homogeneity)
Mechanical performance metrics (tensile/compression tests to assess strength, ductility, and fatigue behavior)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated sample set does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties (along with reduced defect density) compared to the non-preheated baseline, then the hypothesis that preheating improves SLM outcomes is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The study was subject to a few limitations, the foremost of which was the absence of pre-alloyed powder of the desired chemical composition. Thus, mechanical alloyed powder was used instead, which had a few drawbacks of its own. Only small powder quantities with comparatively coarse particle sizes could be established. Therefore, a small PBF-LB machinery able to cope with these conditions was employed, but it lacked the ability to preheat the fabrication chamber. Despite these difficulties, however, the CrFeNiTi MPEA was successfully processed by means of PBF-LB, and samples with large defect-free sections were produced. This serves as a good indicator that this type of alloy is suitable for the PBF-LB process, and with better processing circumstances, significantly larger, defect-free samples should be attainable.

AbstractThe equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (HEA) possesses excellent properties including exceptional strength–ductility synergy, high corrosion resistance, and good thermal stability. Selective laser melting (SLM) additive manufacturing facilitates the convenient fabrication of the CoCrFeNiMn HEA parts with complex geometries. Here, the SLM process optimization was conducted to achieve a high relative density of as-built CoCrFeNiMn HEA bulks. The mechanisms of process-induced defects and process control were elucidated. The microscale mechanical behaviors were analyzed through in situ scanning electron microscopy observation during the compression tests on micro-pillars of the as-built HEA. The stress–strain characteristics by repeated slip and mechanism of “dislocation avalanche” during the compression of micro-pillars were discussed. The high-cycle fatigue tests of the as-built HEA were performed. It was found that a large number of nano-twins were induced by the fatigue, causing a non-negligible cycle softening phenomenon.
